To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hrp genes of Ralstonian solanacearun are under the genetic regulation of a bacterial receptor of plant cell contact.

the expression of Ralstonian pathogenicity genes is specifically induced by the contact with plant cells, that the outer membrane protein PrrA is the first example of bacterial receptor for plant‐cell‐wall signals and that this protein triggers the transcriptional induction by interacting with a transcriptional activator, HrpB.

the outer membrane protein, PrhA, constitutes a bacterial sensor of plant contact, and that it is required for the transcriptional induction, in Ralstonia, of the hrp and type III secretion determinants of bacterial plant pathogenicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a bacterial receptor of a plant cell wall component, the first example of such a receptor in a bacterial plant pathogen.
a bacterial sensor of plant contact that controls the transcriptional activation in the pathogen of genes involved in pathogenicity.
the characterization of the hrp regulon in the plant pathogenic bacterium R. solanacearums and with the identification of the bacterial receptor for a plant signal that activates the hrp regulons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PrhA receptor of R.solanacearum recognizes the plant cell surface and triggers the activation of the transcription of the hrp genes.
the hrpB gene is the first gene to be activated in response to the perception of the plant cell surface by the pathogen, and the PrhA outer membrane protein acts as a sensor of the plant cell wall.
the hrpB gene is induced by the contact of Ralstonium solanacearium bacteria with the plant cell wall.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PrhA is the first bacterial cell‐surface receptor that senses a non‐diffusable signal present in the extracellular matrix of the host plant.
the hrp genes of R. solanacearums are induced in response to plant cell contact through a two‐step signal transduction pathway: the first one involves PrhA and the second one the hrpB gene product.
PrhA is the bacterial sensor of plant contact that controls the transcription of hrpB and the expression of hrp genes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bacterial sensor PrhA, in response to a signal from the plant cell wall, activates the hrpB gene and thereby the hrp gene expression.
the hrpB regulon is specifically induced in the vicinity of the bacterium and not in the bulk of the bacterial culture.
the plant cell wall is a complex mixture of polysaccharides that is recognized by the pathogen through a receptor that triggers the transcription of virulence genes.
